title: Upholstery stain treatment and soil assessment
audience: Upholstery cleaners who assess soils and stains and decide what can be treated.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: ACCC, False or misleading claims (published and last modified 28 June 2026; no date in the body); Safe Work Australia, Hazardous chemicals register (no publication or update date shown; the only date is 2011, the year of the model WHS laws); Safe Work Australia, Using safety data sheets (no publication or update date shown; the only date is 2011, the year of the model WHS laws); Safe Work Australia, How to manage work health and safety risks (code of practice) (copy dated December 2011, as shown on the document; section 4.1).
learningOutcomes: Assess the soil and the stain type before treatment, and record its age and appearance.
Choose a stain treatment that is compatible with the fabric and the test result.
Explain what may not be removable, and avoid promising the removal of a stain.

instruction.heading: Assessing the stain
instruction.body: Start by naming the soil or stain as closely as you can: food, drink, body oil, ink, pet urine, dye transfer from clothing, or a mix. Ask the customer how and when it happened, and record the answer as the customer's account rather than as your own finding. Note the age in hours, days or months, and the appearance: whether the stain is wet, tacky, crusted or dry, whether it has a ring or halo, and how far it reaches. Older and dried stains usually need a different approach from a fresh one. A stain that has been wetted and dried several times may have moved deeper into the fibre or into the padding. Check the care label, if there is one, for the fibre content and any cleaning code. Do not apply heat until the stain has been assessed, because some stains set with heat, and heat can change some fabrics permanently. Photograph the stain before any work, with the customer's permission, in even light.

instruction.heading: Testing before you treat
instruction.body: Choose a hidden test area, such as the underside of a seat cushion or the back of a skirt panel, and test the planned product there first. Watch for colour change, fibre damage, dye bleeding onto the cloth, and any change in feel as the area dries. Give the test time to dry before you judge it, and record the result. If the test area changes, stop and reassess before you touch the stain. For example, if a test patch leaves a light ring after it dries, the product is not suitable for that fabric, and you need a different approach or a referral. A test does not prove the stain will respond, but it does show whether the fabric can take the product at all.

instruction.heading: Choosing and working the treatment
instruction.body: Choose a treatment that is compatible with the fabric and with the result of the test. Remove loose solids gently before any liquid goes on, so that they are not pushed deeper. Work from the outside of the stain inwards to stop it spreading, and blot with a clean white cloth rather than rubbing. Rubbing spreads the stain and roughens the fibre. Use the least product that works, and apply it as the label directs, including dilution, contact time and rinsing or extraction. Do not leave the fabric over-wet, because excess moisture can carry the stain outwards as it dries and can leave a tide mark or an odour. Stop if the fabric starts to change, if the dye begins to move, or if the stain does not respond after the label's contact time. Dry the area as the procedure directs, with air movement, and check it again once it is dry before you decide on the result.

instruction.heading: What may not come out
instruction.body: Explain that some stains may not come out fully. The usual cases are old dye, pet damage, stains that have been set by heat or by an earlier product, and tide lines left by drying. Pet urine can leave an odour and a discolouration in the padding under the fabric, and surface treatment may not reach it. Record the stain and its likely limit before you start, and give the customer the limit in writing. If an odour persists after treatment, refer it to a specialist rather than covering it with fragrance. A fragrance can hide the problem, and it can also create a claim you cannot support.

instruction.heading: Products, labels and safety data
instruction.body: Read the product label and its safety data sheet (SDS) before you use a product. The SDS describes the hazards, first aid and the PPE that the product needs, and you must be able to reach it easily while you work. Keep to the products your business has approved. Do not mix products unless the label allows it, because mixing can create a hazardous reaction. Wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS or label sets. PPE is the lowest level of control, so also keep the amount of product to the minimum, ventilate where the label requires it, and keep bystanders away from the work area.

instruction.heading: What you say about the result
instruction.body: Any claim about the result must be accurate, and you must have reasonable grounds for it when you make it. Do not promise that a stain will be removed, that the fabric will look as new, or that the treatment is guaranteed. Silence can also mislead, so if you know a limit applies, say so before the work starts. Under the consumer rules, intention does not matter: a statement that creates a false impression can breach the rules even if each word is accurate. Describe the expected result as uncertain, for example 'may improve', and record the limit you agreed.

procedure: Identify the stain or soil type as far as possible, and record the customer's account, the age and the appearance.
Check the care label and the fabric, and photograph the stain with permission before any work.
Do not apply heat until the stain has been assessed.
Test the planned product on a hidden area, let it dry, and record the result.
Remove loose solids gently, then work from the outside of the stain inwards with a clean white cloth, blotting rather than rubbing.
Use the least product that works, as the label directs, and avoid over-wetting.
Stop if the fabric changes or the dye moves, and record the point where you stopped.
Dry the area, check the result, and record the limit in writing before the customer signs off.

workedExamples.situation: An old pet stain on a fabric sofa has a persistent odour and a faint discolouration.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you tell the customer, and what do you record before any treatment?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the stain's location, its age as the customer reports it, the odour, and the faint discolouration, with photographs taken with permission. Test a hidden area first. Explain that the old stain and the odour may not fully come out, and that residue in the padding may not be reached by surface treatment. Offer a conservative treatment with approved products, and record the limit in writing. If the odour remains after treatment, refer it to a specialist. Do not promise removal, and do not cover the odour with fragrance.

workedExamples.situation: A fresh red wine spill lands on a light-coloured fabric, and the fibre content is not on the care label.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first step, and what do you avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: Blot the liquid from the outside inwards with a clean white cloth, without rubbing. Do not apply heat, and do not use a hair dryer or heat gun on the stain. Try to identify the fibre, and test a hidden area with the planned product before using it on the stain. If the fibre cannot be identified, or the test changes the fabric, stop and refer the item. Record the time since the spill, the test result and the limit.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks you to guarantee that an ink mark will come out completely.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and what do you write?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not give the guarantee. Explain that the result depends on the ink, how long it has been there and the fabric, and that the test area will show how the fabric responds. Write the expected result as uncertain, record the agreed limit, and confirm it with the customer before you start. A result promised without reasonable grounds can mislead the customer.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved stain-treatment products, each with its label and safety data sheet available at the job.
Clean white cloths for blotting, and a clean water supply.
Labelled spray bottles or dispensers, marked for the dilution the label directs.
Upholstery extraction or vacuum equipment, used as the procedure directs.
Torch held low across the fabric, to show the edges of the stain.
Gloves and eye protection as the SDS sets. These are the lowest level of control and do not replace the controls above them.

commonErrors.error: Applying heat to a stain before it has been assessed.
commonErrors.prevention: Assess the stain first, and confirm the fabric can take the treatment.

commonErrors.error: Rubbing a stain, which spreads it and roughens the fibre.
commonErrors.prevention: Blot from the outside inwards with a clean white cloth.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the hidden test on a fabric that looks familiar.
commonErrors.prevention: Test every fabric and product on a hidden area before it touches the stain.

commonErrors.error: Over-wetting the upholstery, which carries the stain outwards and leaves a tide mark.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the least liquid and product that works, and dry as the procedure directs.

commonErrors.error: Promising full removal of an old stain.
commonErrors.prevention: Explain the limit, write it down, and get the customer's agreement before work starts.

commonErrors.error: Using a product that is not on the approved list, or mixing products.
commonErrors.prevention: Use approved products only, and follow the label and the SDS.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Labels and safety data sheets. Safe Work Australia's guidance says a business holding hazardous chemicals at a workplace should have an SDS for each one, keep copies in a register, and make the SDS easy to reach for workers who use or handle the chemical. The register must list the hazardous chemicals with their current SDS and be kept where workers can reach it.

PPE is the lowest level of control. Safe Work Australia's risk-management code ranks administrative controls and PPE below elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls, and describes PPE as a last resort, an interim measure or a back-up to higher controls (copy dated December 2011, section 4.1; a later edition was not read).

Claims about results. The ACCC states that claims must be accurate and backed by reasonable grounds, that a false impression can breach the rules even when each word is true, and that intention is irrelevant (ACCC, false or misleading claims; page metadata 28 June 2026).
Dilution, dwell time, PPE details for a named product, and the disposal of used cloths and liquid: these come from the product label and SDS.
Stain-specific methods, the blotting sequence, drying times and the treatment of pet odour are general practice.

qualityStandard: The stain is identified and recorded with its age, appearance and the customer's account, and photographs are taken with permission.
A hidden test area is completed, dried and recorded before the stain is treated.
The treatment is chosen from the test result, and blotting runs from the outside inwards with the least product.
The limit of the treatment is written down and agreed; no full removal is promised.
documentationEvidence: Stain assessment record: type, age, appearance, fabric and the customer's account.
Hidden test record: product, area, time and result.
Treatment record: product, dilution as labelled, contact time, method and result.
Written limit statement signed or acknowledged by the customer.
summary: Assess the stain and the fabric before you use heat or any product.
Test a hidden area, then blot from the outside inwards with the least product.
Record the limit in writing, and never promise full removal.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must heat not be applied before the stain has been assessed?
options: Some stains set with heat, and heat can change some fabrics
Heat makes every stain spread outwards across the whole fabric
Heat only slows the treatment down and adds time to the job

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a fresh stain be worked?
options: Rubbed hard from the centre outwards to lift the stain quickly
Blotted from the outside inwards with a clean white cloth
Left to dry before any treatment starts, so the stain sets well

knowledgeChecks.question: An old pet stain still has an odour after treatment. What is correct?
options: Promise the customer that the stain will be removed
Cover the odour with fragrance and say nothing
Record the limit and refer the persistent odour to a specialist
